headlines.article_text: Apple event today: Live updates of foldable iPhone Duo Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Apple kicked off its biggest launch event of the year on Wednesday , with new CEO John Ternus making his big debut. Ternus kicked off the "Surprise and shine" event with a first look at the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, which come in new colors glacier and burgundy. Investors are closely watching to see if Apple raises starting prices for its iPhones during a global computer parts shortage. The company raised prices on Macs and iPads over the summer. Former CEO Tim Cook was in attendance, and Apple customers and investors are watching to see where Ternus follows Cook's footsteps, and where he diverges. The latest from the event: Behold, the foldable iPhone Duo Apple Watch is listening to your conversations More details on the A20 Pro chip You will be paying $100 more for iPhone 18 Pro AI image check with Apple Reference Image The first product launch is the iPhone 18 Pro and Max in new colors Ternus says the iPhone is the best device for AI 3 Min Ago iPhone Duo will cost $1999 iPhone Duo Apple Inc. Apple said its iPhone duo will cost $1,999, in line with competitors and lower than much of what Wall Street was expecting. It will hit store shelves on Oct. 23. — Kif Leswing 11 Min Ago More iPhone Duo details iPhone Duo Apple Inc. Apple's marketing chief Joswiak said that the outer display of the Duo was 90% the screen area of the iPhone 18 Pro, and the inner display is 7.6-inches. The phone will use a fingerprint sensor built into the side button for unlocking. Its case is made out of titanium. Craig Federighi, senior VP of Software Engineering, said that Apple had redesigned much of its iOS software to take advantage of the two screens, moving buttons and other controls. Users can multitask with two apps at the same time and can use Apple's stylus called Pencil. "We looked at every aspect of iOS to see how we could make it even more useful on iPhone Duo," Federighi said. —Kif Leswing 24 Min Ago Here's Apple's foldable phone: iPhone Duo iPhone Duo Apple Inc. It's official, Apple is making a foldable phone. "For a device that plays such a central role in your life, a larger display would open up entirely new possibilities," Ternus said. "We think the best way to achieve that is with a foldable design." He said that other foldables feel like "two phones awkwardly stuck together." Apple's phone is about the size of a passport and has an internal and external screen. iPhone Duo Apple Inc. — Kif Leswing 26 Min Ago No price hike for Apple Watch Apple Watch Series 12 Apple Inc. Apple Watch did not get a price increase. Series 12 will cost $399 and up, and the Ultra 4 starts at $799. Apple also announced a new version of the Apple Watch with a ceramic case. Apple Watch Series 12 — Kif Leswing 28 Min Ago Apple Watch can record and summarize your conversations Apple Watch Audio Intelligence Apple Inc. Apple is making its Apple Watch Series 12 into an AI device with a new feature called Audio Intelligence. The feature will use the Apple Watch's microphone to record conversations and allow the user to review things that were just said. "We've all been in situations where you've missed a key detail of what someone just said and wished you could go back. Now you can use live rewind, which lets you go back in time for 15 seconds," said an Apple representative in the video. It will also be able to summarize your important conversations with a feature called Siri Recap. "It uses ambient listening to take high-level notes of your conversations, like takeaways from a team meeting or a parent-teacher conference. Conversations will have an Apple Intelligence-generated title, summary, and key points," Apple said. Apple said the feature would be private and would not store audio recordings or share them with Apple. The features will be available in beta later this year. — Kif Leswing 32 Min Ago Apple adds lots of new health features to Apple Watch Apple Watch Health monitor Apple Inc. Apple redesigned a lot of the health features in its Health iPhone app with AI-powered coaching. "Each morning, Apple Watch analyzes your recent activity, vitals, and sleep to give you one score with a clear call on your body's capacity to take on the day," Apple's Sumbal Desai said. It's expected to launch later this year. — Kif Leswing 37 Min Ago More details on the A20 Pro, Apple’s first 2nm iPhone chip for better heat controls and on-device AI Apple CEO John Ternus stands on stage at Apple's "Surprise and Shine" event at the company's corporate headquarters, Apple Park, on Sept. 9, 2026 in Cupertino, California. Benjamin Fanjoy | Getty Images Apple unveiled its new A20 Pro system on a chip for iPhone 18 Pro. It's the first high-volume smartphone processor to be made on Taiwan Semiconductor 2 nanometer, the leading chip manufacturer's most advanced node. While 2nm chips can only be made in Taiwan, Apple has committed to make some iPhone chips on TSMC's new fabs in Arizona, too. The A20 Pro is meant to optimize AI on-device, as Apple races to catch up in the AI race by relying on the security and privacy of avoiding the cloud. The A20 Pro is a system on a chip, or SoC, with central and graphics processors and memory integrated together, and it has a dedicated AI accelerator Apple calls a Neural Engine, to optimize that AI on device. The A20 Pro has a six-core CPU that Apple said runs up to 20% faster, with neural accelerators to power low-latency on-device AI workloads. Its new GPU has seven cores for up to a 40% increase in performance. Memory took a big leap too, with a 50% increase in bandwidth and what Apple said is the "widest memory interface we've ever shipped in an iPhone." Apple got there by redesigning the chip to place the core logic silicon side-by-side with the memory chips. Memory optimization is key in the midst of a global memory shortage, as all the biggest players race to secure memory supply from giants SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron. It's also why Apple raised prices on MacBooks and iPads in June. — Katie Tarasov 41 Min Ago Apple announces AirPods 5 Apple AirPods 5 Apple Inc. Apple announced new AirPods models called AirPods 5. These new devices have a longer battery life and have active noise cancellation, which previously wasn't available on the least expensive AirPods. They cost $129, and there's a version with wireless charging that retails for $149. According to Kaiann Drance, vice president of iPhone Marketing, "the number is instantly active on whichever iPhone you pick up." She added that the feature will launch with T-Mobile and Deutsche Telekom, with Verizon and EE adding support by the end of the year. More carriers will follow. — Isabel O'Brien 45 Min Ago iPhone 18 Pro gets a $100 price increase iPhone 18 Pro Apple Inc. Apple's new phones will get a price increase amid a global component shortage, especially for memory. The iPhone 18 Pro will start at $1199, Apple said. That's $100 more than last year's iPhone 17 Pro. The iPhone 18 Pro Max will start at $1299, which is also a $100 hike. The phones go on pre-order on Saturday and will ship on Sept. 18. — Kif Leswing 49 Min Ago Apple introduces feature to prove photo was taken by an iPhone, not made with AI Authenticity check in the new iPhone 18 Pro camera. headlines.title: CoreWeave CEO chalks up public AI pushback to the speed of change: 'And that is frightening'
headlines.summary: CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator spoke to CNBC at the Goldman Sachs' Communacopia + Technology Conference this week.
headlines.article_text: CoreWeave CEO says speed of AI change is 'frightening' the public Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator said he thinks artificial intelligence companies haven't explained the technology's benefits well enough to the public. Those comments came during the Goldman Sachs' Communcacopia + Technology conference, which brings together leaders across the biggest tech and media companies. In this article ANTHR.FG OPENAI.FG CMCSA CHTR Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:22 04:22 CoreWeave CEO: AI industry has not done a good job explaining data center impact on communities Squawk on the Street The public opposition to artificial intelligence and data centers is front and center at the Goldman Sachs Communcacopia + Technology Conference. CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator told CNBC's David Faber that companies haven't explained the technology's benefits well enough to the public. "I don't think we have done a particularly good job of talking about the benefits of what the data centers allow the AI companies to be able to deliver to people, to governments, to decision making," Intrator said in comments that aired Wednesday. The annual conference brings together leaders across the biggest tech and media companies, and AI adoption — along with the pushback many local communities are showing towards its buildout — is perhaps one of the biggest opportunities, and risks, facing businesses of every kind. Intrator insisted that the fear around the transformation isn't about data centers, specifically, but is about how fast things are changing. "It is really about: Hey, you know the world is changing, and it's changing very quickly, and that's going to have impacts on myself. It's going to have impacts on my children, and what is that going to look like? And that is frightening," he added. As Goldman's conference got underway, another set of comments in the tech world caught attention as an AI researcher quit his job at Anthropic Tuesday, warning the rapidly-evolving technology "could kill us all by the end of the decade." Jacob Coxon, who worked at both Anthropic and its chief competitor OpenAI , accused the companies of "gambling with our lives" in the race towards AI superintelligence. "Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing," Coxon wrote in a post on X announcing his resignation. Read more CNBC tech news Apple event live updates: First foldable iPhone, new watch series expected as Ternus makes debut Andreessen- and Thiel-backed defense startup opens U.S. missile factory as it exits stealth Anthropic researcher says AI has more than 10% chance of 'killing all humans' after colleague quits How one hedge-fund manager built his firm to be powered entirely by AI agents Cable companies talk broadband pressure Other disruptions were on the agenda Wednesday, as cable executives continued to forecast competitive pressure on the broadband business. Both Comcast and Charter Communications have seen quarterly broadband customer losses in recent years due to the rise of alternatives, namely fixed wireless, or 5G, providers. On Wednesday, Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong reiterated that those pressures still exist, particularly from fixed wireless. "Satellite looms out there as a potential threat," Armstrong said Wednesday, in addition to competition from fixed wireless. He added that while competition from satellite providers like Starlink isn't necessarily happening yet, "there's no complacency around it." "I think we'll see it over time … in particular in rural and maybe deep suburban markets," Armstrong said of potential satellite competition. Comcast and Charter's stocks were each down more than 5% in midday trading. Comcast and Charter have reworked pricing strategies and leaned on their growing mobile businesses as methods to retain, and potentially gain, more broadband customers in recent years. Armstrong added that, as mentioned during Comcast's second-quarter earnings call, the company is starting to see "irrational competition" when it comes to pricing for fiber broadband and that's continuing into the third quarter. For the period ended June 30, Comcast reported that it once again lost broadband customers, and revenue for the segment dropped due to lower pricing plans and promotions that began to take hold.
